target_customer: Gift givers who want to give small stock or index fund amounts, and the recipients who become investors
problem: Gift cards and cash do not create savers, and buying fractional shares as a gift was awkward. SparkGift sold gift certificates for fractional shares of stocks and index funds starting at 20 dollars.
business_model: Transaction fee of 2.95 dollars plus 3 percent per gift

founders.name: Peggy Mangot
founders.background_notes: YC page lists these roles as past experience and JPMorgan as a later role.

founders.name: Bob Haigler
founders.background_notes: Spelled Hagler on the company site and Haigler on the YC page and press release.

founders.name: Tia Gao
founders.background_notes: Named as a founder on the company site only.

exit.reason: Customers were moved onto Stockpile's brokerage platform.

technical_complexity.rationale: A web checkout plus broker-dealer partner integration is standard engineering. Compliance relied on partners, with sales through Spark Gift Sales LLC and Spark Advisors LLC.

defensibility.rationale: The product was a thin gifting layer over a partner broker-dealer, and Stockpile offered similar stock gift cards, so copying was easy. Registration entities gave only a weak compliance position.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Stockpile acquired SparkGift in June 2016 and moved its customers to its own platform.

market_need_then: The company's pitch was to create new savers through gifts, but no source gives demand data. Its fees of 2.95 dollars plus 3 percent on 20 dollar gifts were high relative to the gift size.

branding.name_origin: The company site says it was formerly called Gratitude Investments before it became SparkGift.
branding.domain_note: Used sparkgift.com, which now redirects to Stockpile messaging. No purchase details found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Friendly gifting language on its own site

rebrands.why: Not stated; the company site mentions only the earlier name

brand_strength.rationale: Press covered only the acquisition. No brand assets or community evidence were found, although the name states the product clearly.

outcome_analysis: SparkGift went through YC Winter 2015, raised a reported 120K seed, and was acquired by Stockpile in June 2016 with its customers moved to the buyer. The price is not public and the press release names no reason beyond fit. Because its fees were high relative to small gifts and a better-known rival sold the same idea, the sale was most likely a soft landing, which is an inference, so treat the failure factor as tentative.
notes: The seed round rests on a single database (CB Insights and trackers repeating it); the company site separately says it raised its seed in March 2015. Investor lists conflict across trackers (Stockpile, Y Combinator, FoundX), and CB shows Stockpile in the acquired round, so only Y Combinator is recorded. Competitors list is empty: Stockpile gift cards are sourced only from a TechCrunch article dated October 2015, seven months after the batch, so it is not listed. YC lists Inactive, which is consistent with the June 2016 acquisition by Stockpile (the product was absorbed), so exit.type is acquisition, not shutdown.
